accepted.question_text: Let M be a compact two-dimensional manifold, let X^r be the space of C^r vector fields on M, let Sigma^r be the subset of C^r-structurally stable vector fields, and let X_1^r = X^r \ Sigma^r with the induced C^r topology. Characterize the subset Sigma_1^r of vector fields in X_1^r that are structurally stable with respect to arbitrarily small perturbations that remain inside X_1^r.

evidence.quote: Consider the complement X1r of the set Σr of C r -structurally stable vector fields, relative to the set X r of all vector fields on a compact two-dimensional manifold. Let X1r be endowed with the induced C r topology. Characterize the set Σr1 of those vector fields that are structurally stable with respect to arbitrarily small perturbations inside X1r .

accepted.question_text: Let X^r be the space of C^r vector fields on the sphere. Is every continuous arc in X^r arbitrarily well approximable by a continuous arc that meets only finitely many bifurcation points, meaning finitely many points outside the set of structurally stable vector fields where qualitative changes occur?

evidence.quote: Prove or disprove that a continuous curve (an arc) in the space X r of vector fields of class C r on the sphere can be arbitrarily well-approximated by a continuous curve that meets only finitely many bifurcation points; that is, points outside the set of structurally stable vector fields, at which qualitative changes occur.
The understanding of the phenomenon of persistent accumulation of bifurcations implies that the problem of the arc as stated above has a negative answer, [42].

accepted.question_text: Do there exist invariant perfect sets, meaning nonempty compact invariant sets that are transversally totally discontinuous, for differential equations of class C^2 on orientable two-dimensional manifolds?

evidence.quote: Do invariant perfect sets (that is, sets that are nonempty, compact, and transversally totally discontinuous) exist for differential equations of class C 2 on orientable twodimensional manifolds?
It was solved in the negative direction by A. J. Schwartz [39].

accepted.question_text: For second-order differential equations of the form x'' = f(x, x'), equivalently for first-order systems x' = y and y' = f(x, y), characterize structural stability and prove the genericity of structural stability in the spirit of Peixoto's results for vector fields on two-dimensional manifolds.

evidence.quote: For equations of the form x00 = f (x, x0 ) (more precisely, for systems of the form x0 = y, y 0 = f (x, y)), characterize structural stability, and prove the genericity of structural stability, in the spirit of Peixoto’s results for vector fields on two-dimensional manifolds.
In [50] I presented a compact version of the solution problem 6.5 in Peixoto’s list.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a compact n-dimensional manifold. If a C^r vector field on M has a nontrivial recurrent orbit through a point p in M, can that vector field be approximated arbitrarily closely in the C^s topology, with s <= r, by another vector field that has a periodic orbit through p?

evidence.quote: This Lemma is in fact an open problem whose statement for class C s and dimension n is as follows: “Every C r vector field on a compact n-dimensional manifold M having a non trivial recurrent through p ∈ M orbit can be arbitrarily approximated in the C s , s ≤ r, topology by one which has through p a periodic orbit.”
Later he extended his analysis for arbitrary n. Carlos Gutierrez made remarkable contributions to the case of n = 2, s > 1, where, it is still open, in most non- orientable surfaces [15].

needs_review.question_text_raw: Use combinatorial invariants to classify the connected components of the open set of structurally stable vector fields. The essential difficulty of this problem is to determine when two structurally stable vector fields agree up to a homeomorphism that preserves their orbits and is isotopic to the identity.

evidence.quote: Use combinatorial invariants to classify the connected components of the open set of structurally stable vector fields.
The essential difficulty of this problem is to determine when two structurally stable vector fields agree up to a homeomorphism that preserves their orbits and is isotopic to the identity.
Some years later, Peixoto himself worked on this problem, [33].
